source: Haddad & Seibel (2025) Functional decomposition of technical products based on large language models and Monte Carlo tree search (ICED25)
finding: First full read of the MCTS-FD paper. GPT-4o was prompted with 21 Roth general functions, rules and 3 worked examples (coffee machine with grinder, Bluetooth speaker, toaster), and asked for a JSON function graph for 50 products. MCTS-FD adds tree search with self-refinement that detects semantic errors (for example an 'add' node with one input) and disconnected parts. It roughly doubled graph validity over plain GPT-4o.
numbers: 50 products per model. Plain GPT-4o: 100% correct format, 44% fully connected, 16% error-free. GPT-4o + MCTS-FD: 100% format, 72% connected, 42% error-free, 0.9 errors per graph, about 21 nodes and 19 edges per graph. Llama 3.1 405B: 86% format, 40% connected, 10% error-free. Llama 8B: 0% error-free.
limits: The 'errors' are rule checks on the graph (node arity, connectivity). Nothing was compared with expert Stone-and-Wood structures, so sub-function recall and flow accuracy are NOT measured. Uses Roth's 21 functions, not the Functional Basis verb-object set, so the vocabulary question is untested. Table 2 text is garbled in the PDF; the figures above are the ones the running text states. MCTS-FD uses many more calls than plain GPT-4o and the paper does not match tokens.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of O3 on engineering products. A cheap checker (arity and connectivity) plus a refine loop lifted validity. Shows a code check on the decomposition itself is feasible. It does not show the decomposition helps solve anything.

source: Haddad & Seibel (2025) ICED25, qualitative rating (same paper)
finding: Graduate students rated function structures blind in a survey. Plain GPT-4o scored as high as or higher than student groups on completeness and logic. Adding MCTS-FD scored lower than plain GPT-4o on both. Students were most creative.
numbers: 20 student decompositions submitted, 8 dropped for major errors or incompleteness, 12 rated. Completeness: GPT-4o 3.96, students 3.91, GPT-4o+MCTS-FD 3.53. Logic: GPT-4o 4.00, students 3.87, MCTS-FD 3.69. Creativity: students 3.48, MCTS-FD 3.32, GPT-4o 3.12 (5-point Likert). Number of raters not stated in the text read.
limits: Raters were course students who also made the entries (peer rating). 8 of 20 student entries were unusable, so the human baseline is weak. No significance tests. Humans and models drew different products.
agent_relevance: The rule-based gain (d01) did not carry over to human-rated quality: the search variant was rated worse. Do not treat a checker score as proof of a better decomposition.

source: Atilola (2014/2015) PhD thesis, Georgia Tech: The effects of representation and analogy on engineering idea generation, Study 3 (basis of Atilola, Tomko & Linsey 2016, Design Studies 42:110-136)
finding: Opened the thesis chapter. Showing a poor example (gas-powered peanut sheller) as a function tree did not cause fixation and gave less fixation than showing it as a sketch. The function tree was NOT better than the no-example control. Sketch plus function tree together gave the most fixation to example features. The function-tree group had the highest design quality.
numbers: N = 61 sophomores and juniors (39 + 22), 4 conditions of 15, 15, 15, 16 (one removed, had seen the task). Non-redundant ideas: Kruskal-Wallis chi2=2.19, p=0.083 (omnibus not significant); sketch vs control p=0.038; function tree vs sketch p=0.043; function tree vs control n.s. Repeated example features: sketch vs control p<0.001, sketch+tree vs control p<0.001, function tree vs control p=0.127. Quality: function tree beat the other three at p=0.036 to 0.043, omnibus p=0.08. Novelty and variety: no differences (p=0.859, 0.991).
limits: The tree shown was the decomposition of someone else's example, not the participant's own decomposition. Pairwise Mann-Whitney values are reported with Z values that look too small for the p values given (for example Z=-1.21 with p=0.043), omnibus tests are mostly not significant, and there is no multiplicity correction. One task, one example, students. The journal paper was behind a paywall and was not opened.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 only for humans and only for a shown decomposition: a function-level view of a prior answer is a safer anchor than the answer itself, and showing both side by side is worst. For the agent: if prior attempts are shown, show them as functions without means, never next to the full answer. This is not a test of whether the agent's own decomposition narrows its answers.

source: Kurfman, Stock, Stone, Rajan, Wood (2001, 2003) Functional modeling experimental studies; Experimental studies assessing the repeatability of a functional modeling derivation method (Missouri S&T ScholarsMine records)
finding: Opened only the repository abstract pages; the full-text PDF is behind a bot check ('Just a moment', HTTP 403). The 2003 abstract says three experiments with a participant pool of mixed skill tested whether the derivation method gives repeatable models, and that results show the method is largely successful with key strengths and improvement areas.
numbers: No participant counts or agreement percentages could be recovered. Abstract only.
quote: Results indicate the method is largely successful and identify its key strengths as well as opportunities for improvement.
limits: Gap 3 stays open. The abstract frames the result as 'largely successful', not as a measured agreement rate, and it tests repeatability between designers, not whether decomposition improves designs.
agent_relevance: Do not cite any agreement figure for the Stone-Wood method. Repeatability between people is the only founding evidence and its numbers are unavailable to us.

source: Atilola, Tomko & Linsey (2016) Design Studies 42, abstract-level report via search result
finding: Search summary of the journal paper matches the thesis chapter: function trees did not induce fixation versus control and reduced it versus sketches.
numbers: Pages 110-136. No numbers beyond the thesis (d03).
limits: Not opened (publisher page returns HTTP 403). Second-hand summary only.
agent_relevance: Use d03 for numbers, not this line.

source: Light, Cheng, Riviere, Wu, Oyamada et al. (2025) DISC: Dynamic Decomposition Improves LLM Inference Scaling (arXiv 2502.16706 v3)
finding: DISC recursively splits a solution into prefix and suffix steps and spends more samples on the steps that matter. It was tested against best-of-N and fixed token or line splits at matched sample budgets and matched token budgets. It gives small gains for gpt-4o-mini and larger relative gains for weaker models. It decomposes the solution trace, not the problem into functions.
numbers: APPS competition subset 200 problems, MATH500, LiveCodeBench 108 problems (Oct-Dec 2024). Pass@10 error proportion: APPS 0.50 to 0.475, MATH500 0.15 to 0.14, LiveCodeBench 0.57 to 0.51 (relative error cut 5.0%, 6.7%, 10.5% over best baseline). LLaMA pass@10 0.01 to 0.04; Qwen 0.095 to 0.17. R1: over 85% relative gain at 10 samples; 33% relative gain at the token budget of one base sample.
quote: the gains from decomposition and step-wise control diminish
limits: Needs a reward signal (ORM or tests, or LLM-written tests: 54% relative gain in that setting). Small test sets, no confidence intervals seen. Absolute gains on gpt-4o-mini are 1 to 6 points. Authors state gains shrink on trivial or non-compositional tasks. A reasoning model appears in one figure only.
agent_relevance: Best token-matched evidence here that adaptive splitting beats plain sampling at equal tokens, including for a reasoning model. Supports O3 as a budget allocator (split where uncertain) more than as an up-front plan. Partly answers gaps 1 and 5.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation (PlanSearch, arXiv 2409.03733)
finding: Searching over short natural-language plans, then coding each plan, gave far more diverse solutions than repeated sampling. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached pass@200 of 77.0% on LiveCodeBench against 60.6% for repeated sampling and 41.4% for the best single pass. Diversity of plans predicts the search gain across models and benchmarks.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, HumanEval+, MBPP+. Backtranslated correct sketches (even 10 tokens long) greatly raise solve rate. Compute-normalised: repeated sampling uses about 244 generated tokens per completion, PlanSearch about 1,428. PlanSearch only wins once the budget is at least about 10,000 tokens per problem. It often lowers pass@1 (for example Sonnet 3.5 on LiveCodeBench). On o1-mini it trails repeated sampling at low k and only slightly beats it at high k; the benchmark is over 90% solved there.
limits: Plans are solution ideas, not function structures. Pass@k values are in plots (exact values not in the text). Code tasks with tests only.
agent_relevance: Directly answers gap 5 for code: the gain comes from plan diversity and a correct sketch, but the token-matched break-even is high (10k tokens) and the gain is small or absent on a strong reasoning model. Argues for O3 only when the agent can afford many attempts, and for varying plans, not one plan.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick & Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting (arXiv 2506.07142)
finding: Step-by-step prompting helps non-reasoning models a little and adds almost nothing for dedicated reasoning models while costing 20 to 80% more time. Many recent models already reason without being asked.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, 25 trials per question per condition. Reasoning models o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5: almost no significant changes; only o4-mini gained at the 51% correct threshold (risk difference 0.056, p=.003); Flash 2.5 fell at the 100% and 90% thresholds (-0.131, p<.001; -0.071, p=.016). CoT requests took 10 to 20 s (20 to 80%) longer for reasoning models, 5 to 15 s (35 to 600%) for others.
limits: Tests generic 'think step by step', not an explicit decomposition step. One benchmark (multiple choice, knowledge-heavy). Early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Sets the prior for gap 1: on a strong reasoning model a forced extra thinking-out step probably gives about zero at a time cost. An O3 gate should default off for such models and be switched on only by a measured task feature.

source: Teng et al. (2025) Atom of Thoughts for Markov LLM Test-Time Scaling (arXiv 2502.12018 v4)
finding: Repeatedly decomposes a question into a dependency graph, then contracts it into a smaller equivalent question. Reported best on every benchmark, including reasoning models, but compute was not matched in the main table.
numbers: Pass rate or F1. o3-mini: AIME 79.6 (CoT) to 83.0 (AoT), LiveCodeBench 23.6 to 32.2, LongBench 56.3 to 65.3. DeepSeek-R1: AIME 78.3 to 81.7. GPT-4o-mini: MATH 78.3 to 83.6, GSM8K 90.9 to 95.0. Max chain length 3. Self-checks: answer equivalence kept in over 99% of contractions, complexity cut 74 to 82% (both judged by an LLM).
limits: The baseline gaps follow a very regular pattern across methods; treat as one group's report, not replicated. Quality metrics are LLM-judged. Cost-efficiency is argued in figures, not matched tokens in Table 1. AoT rewrites the question; it is not a function structure.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a decompose-then-contract loop helps even strong reasoning models, but unreplicated and with unmatched cost. Candidate for the O3 test in gap 1.

source: Teng et al. (2025) Atom of Thoughts, ablation and structure analysis (same paper, section 4.3 and appendix B.3)
finding: Two ablations hurt: removing the decomposition, and keeping decomposition but dropping the DAG-guided contraction. The second hurt more. The authors say partial or superficial structure can be worse than none. Accuracy fell as the solution graph got deeper or had more sub-questions.
numbers: Typical question: depth 2 to 4 (3 most common), 2 to 5 sub-questions (3 to 4 most common). Max transition count fixed at 3. Accuracy trends down with depth and sub-question count (scatter plots; no coefficient given).
limits: Ablation shown as a figure only; no numbers in the text. Single group.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 7: a poor or half-enforced decomposition can do harm, which fits the Booth null. Supports a quality gate on the decomposition before use. Also gives a working size rule: most problems split into 3 to 4 parts at depth 3, and more than that predicts lower accuracy.

source: Zhou, Pujara, Ren, Chen, Cheng, Le, Chi et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures (arXiv 2402.03620)
finding: The model picks, adapts and implements reasoning modules once per task into a structure, then follows it per instance. It beat CoT and self-consistency with 10 to 40 times fewer calls per instance. It helped most on tasks that need world knowledge.
numbers: BBH tasks; GPT-4 and PaLM 2-L. Self-Discover needs 1 call per instance plus 3 task-level calls, against 10 for CoT self-consistency and 40 for majority voting over 40 reasoning modules.
limits: Output longer than CoT, so tokens per call are higher; calls are not tokens. 2023 models. The structure is a plan of reasoning steps, not a function decomposition.
agent_relevance: A per-task plan made once and reused is cheap. This fits one decomposition per task type, not per attempt. Does not settle token-matching (gap 5).

source: Erdogan, Lee, Kim, Moon, Furuta, Anumanchipalli, Keutzer, Gholami (2025) Plan-and-Act (arXiv 2503.09572 v3)
finding: A planner/executor split improved web agents, but only with a good planner. An untrained planner did not help executors that had been trained, and its plans could confuse them.
numbers: WebArena-Lite: doubling executor trajectory data gave only 0.61%. Adding replanning gave +10.31% over the static planner, reaching 53.94%. With an untrained base executor, a dynamic high-quality plan gave +34.39% to 44.24%. With CoT in the planner: 57.58% (Llama 3.3 70B). Full WebArena 45.7 to 48.15%. WebVoyager 81.36% (QwQ-32B).
limits: The planner is fine-tuned on synthetic plans, so this is training, not scaffolding. Environment reward and held trajectories used. Plan quality not scored separately from final success.
agent_relevance: For gaps 5 and 7: plan quality matters, a poor plan hurts a capable executor, and a replan step was worth more than the first plan. Argues that O3 needs a re-decompose path when a sub-problem fails.

source: Dual-CoT for small language models (arXiv 2604.25039), via search summary
finding: Search summary reports that prompted multi-step reasoning in a small model was far below a direct-answer baseline before fine-tuning.
numbers: 24% against 78% for the direct baseline (second-hand; paper not opened).
limits: Not opened. Second-hand summary of one abstract passage. Small models only.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that forcing steps on a model not trained for it can cost accuracy (gap 6). Needs the paper before use.

source: Haddad & Seibel (2025) related-work section on automatic function-structure generation (AutoFunc, association rules, PDDL planning)
finding: The ICED25 related work lists non-LLM routes: AutoFunc (no longer maintained), association-rule mining of repository data, and plan-based derivation with Roth's 30 functions as PDDL actions. It notes that decompositions built as knowledge graphs share structure with planning problems.
numbers: No benchmark numbers given for these routes in the text read.
limits: Review text only; the cited papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: No standard benchmark of function-structure generation exists. Our own test (gap 2) would need expert structures as reference, which have to be built by hand.

source: Kurfman et al. (2000) Theoretical Underpinnings of Functional Modeling: Preliminary Experimental Studies, via repository record and search summary
finding: Search summary: design teams and individuals built functional models for a toaster, a power screwdriver and a toy dart gun, with and without the formalisms, at three universities. Described as very repeatable, with weaknesses in the formalisms noted.
limits: Not opened beyond the title record; full text blocked.
agent_relevance: Same as d04: no usable agreement figure.
